messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Public Transport: Bus riding, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Leo was twenty-four when the man he loved broke his nose. It happened in the small apartment they shared, after an argument about something Leo could no longer remember—only the feeling of the first blow, a closed fist against his cheekbone, and the second, harder, to his ribs. He had frozen, unable to fight back or run, telling himself it was a mistake, that Danny would stop, that it was his fault for pushing too hard. The memory never felt like something that had ended. Even now, three years later, when it surfaced—triggered by a crowded bus, by the weight of a male colleague’s hand on his shoulder, by a news story about domestic violence—Leo felt the impact in his body again: the sharp crack along his cheekbone, the bruising ache in his ribs, a wave of nausea so intense he had to stop whatever he was doing. He would stand in the middle of a city sidewalk or lock himself in the office restroom, pressing his palms against the cool tile until his breathing slowed, convinced that Danny was still there, that the attack was happening right now.

The consequences of that night bled into every corner of Leo’s life. He worked as a journalist for a local paper, and his beat required him to take the bus across town for interviews. But buses had become unbearable. The press of bodies, the sudden jostle when the driver braked, the way a man standing too close could lean into his space—all of it sent his heart into a gallop and made his skin crawl. He had started driving instead, a longer commute that left him exhausted and late for deadlines. His editor had noticed the drop in his output; Leo made excuses about traffic, about family issues, never the truth. More damaging was his avoidance of one-on-one conversations with male sources. He would find ways to bring a colleague along, or reschedule, or pitch stories that could be handled over email. His professional network was narrowing, and he knew it, but the idea of being trapped in a room with a man he didn’t fully trust felt like an invitation to disaster.

At home, Leo’s girlfriend Maya tried to be patient, but she could not understand why he would wake at 3 A.M. to check the locks—again—or why he barely touched the dinner she cooked. He had developed a rigid control over food, skipping meals or eating just enough to avoid suspicion, because the only thing he could manage in his life was the discipline of hunger. He never let himself feel anger. When Maya pushed him to talk about what was wrong, he would go silent, turning the accusation inward: he had done something wrong, he had provoked Danny, he was inadequate, unworthy of love, too weak to protect himself. These thoughts looped endlessly, especially at night, when the quiet pressed in and every creak of the building meant someone was coming.

The smallest delays undid him. A subway delay, a late reply to a text—Leo’s mind would jump immediately to catastrophe: Maya had been hurt, his boss was firing him, someone was waiting around the corner. He could not trust anyone’s reassurances. “You’re safe now,” Maya would say, and he would nod, but his body did not believe her. He had learned that people could smile while planning to hurt you; Danny had smiled the day before the attack, had bought him flowers. Trust was a luxury he could no longer afford.

What finally brought Leo to a therapist’s office was a panic attack on the bus last week, triggered by a man who looked like Danny from behind—just the shape of his shoulders—and the memory hit so hard that Leo vomited onto the floor. The driver pulled over, someone called an ambulance, and for hours Leo sat in an ER, humiliated and trembling, unable to explain why a bus trip had undone him. Maya had begged him to get help. So he came, not because he believed anything would change, but because he could not keep living like this—jumping at shadows, starving his own body, shrinking his world to a handful of safe places. He was afraid the therapist would tell him he was broken beyond repair. He was also afraid that she might be right.
